lead: A serviceable aircraft, a healthy crew, and still it flies into a hill. That is controlled flight into terrain (CFIT), long one of the largest causes of deaths in jet aviation. The cure is a warning early enough to climb away. Terrain awareness and ground proximity warning systems — GPWS, TAWS, EGPWS — compare the aircraft's path with the ground, first only the ground below, later a stored map of the terrain ahead, and call "pull up" early enough to climb away.
prereq: You need the radio altimeter from radar principles, the ILS glide path from landing aids, the GNSS position from satellite navigation, and the barometric altimeter from Air data instruments: airspeed indicator and altimeter.

sections.h3: Why the ground kills: height above ground

blocks.text: In CFIT an airworthy aircraft, under control, is flown into ground, water or an obstacle the crew did not see in time, usually at night or in cloud after a small altitude or track error.

Two heights exist in the cockpit. The barometric altimeter shows height above a pressure datum and cannot know that a hill stands in the way. The radio altimeter times an echo and reads the height above the surface directly below, over roughly 0 to 2500 ft. That reading is radio altitude, RA.

Every reactive warning below is built from RA plus sink rate, airspeed, gear and flap position, and — in one mode only — the ILS glideslope. RA looks straight down, so the warning is late, typically 10 to 30 s before impact, and blind to a ridge 5 km ahead.

Classic GPWS is a set of seven modes. Each mode is an envelope: a limit that changes with RA, not a fixed number. Early units compared the envelope with barometric sink rate or the rate of change of RA; digital units added airspeed, gear, flap and ILS deviation.

Detects

Too close to the ground, not in landing configuration
TOO LOW GEAR, TOO LOW FLAPS, TOO LOW TERRAIN
Excessive deviation below the glide path

blocks.text: Mode 1 works on barometric sink rate, gated by RA: the allowed sink rate falls as RA falls. Crossing the outer line gives the soft "SINK RATE"; crossing the inner one gives "PULL UP". Mode 2 watches how fast RA is falling, with separate clean and flap-down envelopes because an aircraft on final closes with the ground by design. Mode 3 guards take-off and go-around: losing height before a safe RA is reached gives "DON'T SINK". Mode 4 calls "TOO LOW GEAR", "TOO LOW FLAPS" or "TOO LOW TERRAIN" when the aircraft is low and not in landing configuration.

Mode 5 is the only reactive mode that needs a ground aid: it is armed when an ILS is tuned and the aircraft sits more than about 1.3 dots below the beam at low RA. It says the aircraft is low on the approach, nothing about terrain. Mode 6 is a reminder; Mode 7 gives windshear warning from the airspeed and vertical-path signature.

sections.h3: TAWS: looking ahead with a database

blocks.text: A terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS), also sold as enhanced GPWS, keeps the reactive modes and adds forward-looking terrain avoidance (FLTA). It carries a terrain and obstacle database (the highest elevation in each grid cell, plus known towers), a position from GNSS or the flight management system, and a computer that projects the track, speed and vertical path ahead. It also gives a premature descent alert (too low for the distance from the runway) and paints the terrain on the navigation display. Class A TAWS, for larger airliners, has FLTA, the premature descent alert, the display and the full reactive modes; Class B, for smaller aircraft, has FLTA, the premature descent alert and fewer reactive modes.

Caution is amber, on the display and as a soft voice, about 60 s before predicted impact: "TERRAIN AHEAD". Warning is red with the hard command "TERRAIN, PULL UP" at about 30 s. Alert times vary with manufacturer, speed and phase of flight.

Inhibits exist because a warning that cries wolf gets switched off. Mode 4 changes its envelope by design once the aircraft is in landing configuration, and a TERR INHIBIT switch lets the crew quiet nuisance alerts on a steep approach into a terrain-ringed airfield, flying the approach on the chart alone.

items: Database currency: a new tower, cable or building is invisible until the database is updated, and many wires and unlit obstacles are never mapped.
Position error: a GNSS outage leaving inertial-only position, a wrong datum, or a bad flight-management position puts the predicted path in the wrong place.
It warns; it does not fly. The escape is a maximum-performance climb the pilot must make.

spec.aria: A side view with altitude up to 5000 feet against distance up to 10 nautical miles. Flat ground at 1000 feet rises as a wall to a 3000 foot ridge at 8 nautical miles. A dashed descending path from 5000 feet would strike the ridge face at 2000 feet after 120 seconds. The caution point is at 4 nautical miles and 3500 feet, the warning at 6 nautical miles and 2750 feet, and from the warning a climb of 1500 feet per minute crosses the ridge 500 feet above its top.

examples.question: An aircraft is at 5000 ft above sea level, descending at 1500 ft/min at a ground speed of 240 kt over ground at 1000 ft. A ridge whose top is at 3000 ft begins 8 nm ahead. FLTA gives a caution 60 s and a warning 30 s before predicted impact. (a) Will the path meet the ridge, and when? (b) Where and at what altitude do the caution and the warning come? (c) At the warning, what climb rate clears the ridge top by 500 ft if the climb starts at once, and if it starts 5 s later?
steps: Time to reach the ridge: 8 nm ÷ 240 kt = 0.0333 h = 120 s.
Altitude then: 5000 − 1500 × (120 ÷ 60) = 2000 ft, which is below the 3000 ft top: the path hits the ridge face at 120 s.
Caution, 60 s before: at t = 60 s the aircraft is at 5000 − 1500 × 1.0 = 3500 ft and 4.0 nm from the ridge. "CAUTION TERRAIN" (on some units "TERRAIN AHEAD").
Warning, 30 s before: at t = 90 s it is at 2750 ft and 2.0 nm out. "TERRAIN, PULL UP".
The reactive modes stay quiet all this time: over the 1000 ft ground the radio altitude at the warning is 1750 ft, and 1500 ft/min there is an ordinary approach sink rate.
Escape: to cross the top at 3500 ft the aircraft must gain 750 ft in the 30 s left: 750 ÷ 0.5 min = 1500 ft/min.
With a 5 s delay only 25 s remain: 750 ÷ (25 ÷ 60) = 1800 ft/min.
examples.answer: Yes: the path meets the ridge face 120 s ahead, at 2000 ft. Caution at 3500 ft, 4.0 nm out; warning at 2750 ft, 2.0 nm out. Clearing the top by 500 ft needs 1500 ft/min at once, or 1800 ft/min after a 5 s delay: every second of hesitation costs climb.

examples.question: The altimeter sub-scale is set to 1018 hPa when the local QNH is 1013 hPa. Near the surface 1 hPa is about 27 ft. What does the altimeter show, and which warnings does the error affect?
steps: The setting is 5 hPa too high, so the altimeter over-reads by 5 × 27 = 135 ft: the aircraft is 135 ft lower than it shows ("from high to low, look out below").
The radio altimeter measures the ground directly and is unaffected, so the RA-gated reactive modes are unaffected.
A constant offset does not change a rate, so the Mode 1 sink-rate comparison is unaffected.
Any check that compares barometric altitude with terrain elevation is 135 ft optimistic; that is one reason TAWS also uses GNSS (geometric) altitude.
examples.answer: The altimeter shows about 135 ft too high. Radio-altitude modes and sink-rate comparisons are unaffected; barometric terrain-clearance checks are 135 ft optimistic.

traps: GPWS is reactive and looks down with the radio altimeter; TAWS look-ahead is predictive and needs a terrain database plus a position. Do not swap the two.
Mode 1 (sink rate) uses barometric descent rate gated by RA; Mode 5 (glideslope) needs a tuned ILS and is below-path deviation in dots. Not the same warning.
Quote radio altitude, not barometric altitude, as the gating quantity of Modes 1 to 5. A barometric height of 900 ft over high ground may be 300 ft above the hill.
FLTA is the forward-looking terrain avoidance function; the premature descent alert is a separate TAWS alert for being too low for the distance to the runway.

quiz.q: What does CFIT stand for, and what makes it different from an aircraft failure?
quiz.a: Controlled flight into terrain: an airworthy aircraft under control is flown into ground or an obstacle the crew did not see in time. Nothing has failed mechanically.

quiz.q: Which sensor feeds the reactive GPWS modes, and what quantity does it measure?
quiz.a: The radio (radar) altimeter. It measures height above the surface directly below the aircraft, from about 0 to 2500 ft, and that reading is the radio altitude RA.

quiz.q: Why does Mode 2 have separate flap-up and flap-down envelopes?
quiz.a: On final approach with flaps down the aircraft closes with the ground by design. One clean-configuration limit would be too sensitive on approach or too slack en route; two envelopes keep the clean limit tight and the landing limit loose.

quiz.q: An aircraft flies level at 180 kt ground speed, 300 ft below the top of a ridge 2.5 nm ahead. How long until predicted impact, and which FLTA alert is showing?
quiz.a: Time = 2.5 ÷ 180 h = 50 s. That is less than 60 s but more than 30 s, so the amber caution is on, and the red warning comes 20 s later.

quiz.q: An aircraft flies towards a newly built radio mast that is not in its terrain database. Why does neither the look-ahead nor the reactive GPWS give a timely warning?
quiz.a: Look-ahead compares the predicted path with stored terrain and obstacles; an unmapped mast has no entry, so the path looks clear. The reactive modes see only the surface directly below; a thin mast is a poor reflector and gives no clearance or sink-rate exceedance. Unmapped obstacles are the blind spot of both, which is why database updates and obstacle charts matter.

quiz.q: Why do crews inhibit some terrain alerts on steep approaches into airfields ringed by high ground?
quiz.a: On a steep, curved approach the projected path meets terrain that the aircraft will in fact clear, so alerts fire again and again and would be ignored. Inhibiting keeps trust in the system; the cost is losing those alerts for that approach, so the crew flies the published procedure exactly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Helicopter TAWS uses a shorter look-ahead because a helicopter can stop rather than climb. Synthetic vision draws the same terrain database on the flight display. Search for helicopter TAWS and synthetic vision.
